title: Staged Transparency: Degradation & Fallback Messaging Playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a practical playbook for GTM, sales, and support focused on a ‘staged transparency’ approach to service degradation: how we communicate, what fallbacks we offer, and the narratives that build trust without creating false promises.

TL;DR:
- Problem: Customers panic when endpoints degrade unpredictably or they see unexplained quality drops. Many vendors hide details or give binary ‘down/up’ messages.
- Our approach: progressive transparency + actionable fallbacks. Inform users early, offer graceful degraded modes, and provide clear remediation paths and timelines.
- Outcome: higher perceived reliability, fewer ticket escalations, and stronger enterprise trust.

What is ‘staged transparency’?
- Notify early at low severity with non-alarming copy (e.g., “small response delays in some regions — working on it”).
- Offer opt-in/prominent fallback choices for customers (regional routing, reduced-quality fast path, cached responses).
- Escalate messaging and support actions as severity and scope grow. Always pair notifications with the next-best-action the customer can take.

Fallback taxonomy (practical options we expose in GTM conversations):
1) Model variant fallback (automatic): switch to smaller/quantized model with same API contract. Use when latency spikes but correctness is not safety-critical.
2) Regional routing (automatic or customer-configurable): route to another region where capacity exists.
3) Degraded-response mode (configurable): return shorter summaries, lower token budgets, or non-streaming fast path. Presented as a deliberate mode customers can enable for reliability.
4) Cache-first responses (transparent): serve cached completions or previously validated responses for repeated prompts (good for knowledge-base queries).
5) Queue-then-respond (honest SLO): place requests into a short delayed queue with ETA, rather than dropping them.

Customer-facing messaging primitives (examples to copy/adapt):
- Proactive banner (low severity): “Performance disruption in <region>. You may see slower responses — our automatic fallbacks are active to keep your app responsive.”
- In-product toast (medium severity): “Switching to low-latency fallback — responses will be shorter but faster. Toggle this off in Settings.”
- Outage email (high severity): subject: “Service update: degraded throughput in <region> — timeline & actions”. Body must include impact, affected endpoints, mitigation in place, ETA for next update, and immediate workarounds.
- Sales elevator (30s): “We design for graceful degradation: when demand or a hardware failure threatens latency, Redwood automatically routes traffic and can switch to validated fallback models. That keeps your product responsive while preserving correctness for critical paths.”

Incident narratives for different audiences (short scripts)
- Developer / API user (proactive Slack/email): “We detected increased tail latency for model-X in us-west-2. We’ve enabled automatic model-variant fallback and regional routing; most requests should be back to normal. If you see errors, please enable ‘degraded-response’ mode in the Console for maximum responsiveness.”
- Product manager (phone): “We’re seeing capacity pressure in Region A due to an autoscaler regression. We’ve triggered cross-region spillover and a quantized model fallback. This affects long-form completions primarily — chat flows remain intact. Expected recovery: 1–2 hours; we’ll update every 30 minutes.”
- Executive / customer success (email): “You may receive higher latency or shorter outputs temporarily. We’re applying an automated fallback that preserves intent but reduces token usage. SLA implications: for Dedicated customers we’re operating under our fallback policy; we’ll follow up with a detailed postmortem.”

Competitive analysis notes (quick bullets — what customers ask and how competitors behave):
- Vendor A (managed-first): often returns HTTP 500 or 502 without fallback options; customers forced to retry and throttle themselves. Pain: bursty apps get poor UX.
- Vendor B (self-hosted runtime): provides options but requires manual ops to flip variants or route regions; high engineering overhead for customers.
- Vendor C (API with opaque errors): hides degradation causes, undermining trust.

Redwood differentiation (how to position):
- Automatic and policy-driven fallbacks that are API-compatible (no code changes).
- Multi-layered fallbacks: runtime (model variant), network (region routing), UX (degraded-response), and cache (prefix/KB).
- Observability tied to messaging: token-level latency breakdowns and templated customer communications for rapid trust-building.

Guidance for sales discovery questions (what to ask customers):
- Which flows can tolerate trimmed outputs (summaries) vs. which require full fidelity?
- Do you have region-specific data residency constraints? (If yes, highlight Private options and routed fallbacks.)
- How important is predictable tail-latency vs. absolute throughput for your product?

Example objection handling (short):
- Customer: “I don’t want my model behavior to change.”
  - Response: “Fallback models are validated against your prompt set and can be pinned per-route; they preserve intent and are temporary — and we report any quality deltas so you can accept or force a failover.”
- Customer: “Will this impact my SLAs?”
  - Response: “We have explicit fallback policies in contracts: Dedicated customers get prioritized cross-region capacity and visibility into fallbacks; hosted tiers get automatic fallbacks with best-effort guarantees. We can map this into contract language for renewals.”

UI copy examples (unique phrasing you can reuse):
- Toggle label: “Enable continuous low-latency mode (may shorten outputs)”
- Banner: “Heads up — we’re temporarily serving condensed responses to keep your app snappy.”
- Support note: “If you rely on verbatim outputs, lock this route to ‘High-fidelity’ — otherwise enable ‘Resilient’ for better uptime.”

Enablement checklist for GTM & CS (what to ship to customers):
- One-pager for sales summarizing fallback types and contract impact.
- Battle-cards for AE and CSM with 3 incident narratives and Q&A.
- Console UX copy and default toggle state.
- A pre-written proactive email template and postmortem template (for high-severity incidents).

Open questions / action items (working notes):
- Validate fallback model quality on 3 representative customer prompt sets (owner: Applied ML).
- Draft contract language for Dedicated customers describing cross-region failover and measurable SLA exceptions (owner: Legal/Rev Ops).
- Build console switch prototypes for ‘Resilient vs. High-fidelity’ modes (owner: Product Console).

FAQ snippets for customer portal (short answers):
- Q: What happens to accuracy when a fallback is used?
  A: Fallbacks are validated to preserve intent. Some verbosity or nuance may be reduced depending on mode; we surface diffs in the Console.
- Q: Can I opt out?
  A: Yes — per-route settings allow you to pin model version and disable automatic region routing.

Appendix: example proactive email (copy you can paste)
Subject: Temporary performance mode active — what we’ve done and how it affects you
Body: Hi <name>,
We’re reaching out because we detected increased latency in <region> yesterday afternoon that could impact completions. To keep your application responsive we enabled an automatic fallback (low-latency model variant + cross-region routing). Most customers see shorter responses but faster throughput. We do not expect data to be re-routed outside of your configured residency boundaries. Next update: in 60 minutes. If this mode would break a critical workflow for you, reply and we’ll prioritize a targeted rollback.

Notes to self (internal tone):
- Keep scripts short and concrete. Customers want actions, not technical minutiae.
- Avoid absolutes like ‘never’ or ‘always’ in public comms.
- Track perception: run a small post-incident NPS pulse when incidents involve fallback modes.

End of document.
